issues.legal_issue: A female donee of a Hindu widow’s pre-1956 transfer did not become an absolute owner under the later enlargement of female Hindu estates unless she was herself a limited owner.
material_facts: A Hindu widow transferred by gift the entire estate she had inherited from her husband to her daughter in 1954.
The daughter possessed the property when the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
The transfer was contrary to the restrictions on alienation under the Hindu law then in force.
issues.conclusion: The daughter did not become a limited owner through the gift and could not acquire absolute ownership under section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 14(1), read as a whole with its Explanation and section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, enlarges the estate of a female Hindu who was a limited owner and possessed the property; it does not enlarge the interest of an alienee who was not a limited owner. The Court applied Bai Vijia v. Thakorbhai Chelabhai, (1979) 3 SCC 300, and Eramma v. Verrupana, (1966) 2 SCR 626, and disapproved Smt. Chinti v. Smt. Daultu, AIR 1968 Delhi 264. It also explained that Gummalapura Taggina Matada Kotturuswami v. Setra Veeravva, AIR 1959 SC 577, concerned a widow’s constructive possession, not an alienee’s entitlement.

rule.if: succession_property_dispute and pre_act_transfer_by_widow and transfer_exceeded_permissible_limits and female_donee_possessed_property_when_law_changed

predicates.succession_property_dispute: The dispute concerns the ownership or succession to property held by a female Hindu.
predicates.pre_act_transfer_by_widow: A Hindu widow transferred property before the change in the law governing female Hindu estates.
predicates.transfer_exceeded_permissible_limits: The widow’s transfer went beyond the purposes or limits permitted under the Hindu law then in force.
predicates.female_donee_possessed_property_when_law: A female recipient of the transfer possessed the property when the later law governing female Hindu estates took effect.

issues.definition: When a succession property dispute concerns a female donee who possessed property under a pre-change transfer by a widow that exceeded permissible limits, the donee does not gain absolute ownership from the later enlargement of female Hindu estates.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-1956 gift of a Hindu widow’s entire inherited estate that was not permitted under Hindu law did not bind the reversioners, who could claim the property after the widow’s death.
material_facts: A Hindu widow gifted her entire inherited estate to one of her daughters in 1954.
The gift was found to be contrary to the restrictions on alienation under the Hindu law then in force.
After the widow died, another daughter claimed the property as a reversioner.
issues.conclusion: The gift did not bind the reversioner, and the donee acquired no title against the reversioner under the gift.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Hindu law applicable before 1956, a widow could alienate her estate for legal necessity or other permitted purposes, but an alienation beyond those limits could be avoided by the reversioners. The widow remained bound by the transfer, while the transfer did not bind the reversioners. The Court relied on Collector of Masulipatam v. Cavaly Vencata, (1861) 8 M.I.A. 529; Natwarlal Punjabhai v. Dadubhai Manubhai, AIR 1954 SC 61; Kamala Devi v. Bachu Lal Gupta, (1957) SCR 453; Radhey Krishan Singh v. Shiv Shankar Singh, (1973) 2 SCC 472; and Radha Rani v. Hanuman Prasad, AIR 1966 SC 216.

rule.if: succession_property_dispute and pre_act_transfer_by_widow and transfer_exceeded_permissible_limits and widow_has_died and reversioner_claims_property

predicates.succession_property_dispute: The dispute concerns succession to property held by a female Hindu.
predicates.pre_act_transfer_by_widow: A Hindu widow transferred property before the change in the law governing female Hindu estates.
predicates.transfer_exceeded_permissible_limits: The widow’s transfer went beyond the purposes or limits permitted under the Hindu law then in force.
predicates.widow_has_died: The widow who made the transfer has died.
predicates.reversioner_claims_property: A person claiming the property as a reversioner asserts a right to it.

issues.definition: If a widow has died after making a pre-change transfer that exceeded permissible limits and a reversioner claims the property, the transfer does not bind the reversioner and the reversioner may claim the property.

issues.legal_issue: Adverse possession against a Hindu widow during her lifetime did not defeat the reversioners’ right to claim property after her death.
material_facts: The daughter possessed the property under the widow’s gift deed.
The gift deed was not permitted under the Hindu law then in force.
The daughter relied on adverse possession against the widow, while the other daughter claimed as a reversioner after the widow’s death.
issues.conclusion: Even if the donee’s possession was adverse to the widow, that possession did not give the donee title against the reversioners or prevent them from claiming the property after the widow’s death.
issues.legal_principle: Where a Hindu widow alienated property without legal necessity, the reversioners were not required to bring a declaratory suit during her lifetime; they could wait until her death and sue the alienee for possession, treating the alienation as a nullity. The Court relied on Radha Rani v. Hanuman Prasad, AIR 1966 SC 216.

predicates.reversionary_property_claim: The proceeding concerns a claim to property by a person asserting a reversionary interest.
predicates.possession_under_unpermitted_widow_trans: The possessor holds property under a transfer made by a widow that was not permitted under the governing Hindu law.
predicates.adverse_possession_claimed_only_against_: The possessor relies on adverse possession against the widow who made the transfer, rather than against the reversioner.
predicates.reversioner_claims_after_widow_death: The reversioner asserts the claim to the property after the widow’s death.

issues.definition: When a possessor relies only on adverse possession against a widow who made an unpermitted transfer, that claim does not defeat a reversioner’s claim made after the widow’s death.
